title: How does Java classloading work (Bootstrap → Platform → Application loaders, delegation model), and can two classes with the same fully-qualified name coexist in one JVM (yes: if loaded by different classloaders, as in app servers/plugins)?
shortTitle: How does Java classloading work, and can two classes with the same name coexist in one JVM?
keyPoints: Class loaders form a hierarchy: Bootstrap (native, loads java.base), Platform (standard modules), and Application (classpath/module path).
The parent-delegation model means a loader asks its parent first and only loads the class itself if the parent cannot.
A class's identity in the JVM is the pair of its fully-qualified name plus its defining class loader.
Two classes with the same name loaded by different class loaders are distinct types with separate Class objects and static fields.
Application servers give each web app its own class loader for isolation, which is why two apps can bundle different library versions.
Class-loader leaks happen when something outside an app holds a reference to its loader, preventing garbage collection on undeploy.

s1_definition.oneliner: Class loaders form a delegating hierarchy (Bootstrap, Platform, Application), and a class's identity is its name plus its loader, so the same class name loaded by different loaders yields distinct, coexisting classes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Bootstrap loader** – native code, loads core `java.base` classes like `Object` and `String`; represented as `null`.
- **Platform loader** – loads other standard JDK modules not in the bootstrap set.
- **Application loader** – loads your classpath or module path; returned by `ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader()`.
- **Parent-delegation** – a loader asks its parent first; only loads itself if the parent fails. Core classes are always from Bootstrap.
- **Class identity** – fully-qualified name plus defining loader. Same name, different loaders, means distinct classes.
- **Isolation** – app servers and plugin systems use separate loaders so deployments do not clash.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of class loaders as a chain of librarians at National Bank of India. When a clerk requests a document, the junior librarian asks the senior, who asks the chief. Only if the seniors do not have it does the junior fetch his own copy. The bank identifies a document by both its title and which librarian issued it. Two documents titled "Fee Policy" from two different librarians are two genuinely different documents. That is how two versions of a plugin run side by side.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Class Loader Hierarchy:

  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │    Bootstrap Loader          │  java.lang.Object, String
  │    (native code, null)       │  java.base module
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │ parent
  ┌──────────▼──────────────────┐
  │    Platform Loader           │  java.sql, java.xml, etc.
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │ parent
  ┌──────────▼──────────────────┐
  │    Application Loader        │  Your classpath / module path
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │ child loaders
  ┌──────────▼───┐  ┌──────────▼───┐
  │ App1 Loader  │  │ App2 Loader  │  (Tomcat per-app)
  │ Jackson 2.14 │  │ Jackson 2.17 │
  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘

  Class Identity:
  name + loader = unique class
  Same name + different loader = different class
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java classloading happens lazily and is performed by a hierarchy of class loaders. The Bootstrap loader loads core `java.base` classes. The Platform loader loads standard JDK modules. The Application loader loads your classpath. They cooperate through parent delegation: a loader asks its parent first and only loads a class itself if the parent cannot. This guarantees core classes always come from Bootstrap.

The crux is the identity rule. A class in the JVM is identified by the pair of its fully-qualified name and its defining class loader. Two classes with the same name loaded by different loaders are distinct types with separate `Class` objects, separate static fields, and are not assignment-compatible. This is the foundation of isolation: Tomcat gives each web app its own loader so they bundle different library versions without conflict.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj used this for a plugin platform where two business units shipped a fee-policy class with the same name but different logic. Each plugin got its own child class loader, so both classes coexisted as distinct types. The senior caution is class-loader leaks: if a `ThreadLocal`, a cache, or a registered JDBC driver holds a reference into an app's loader, that loader cannot be collected on undeploy, slowly exhausting metaspace.

Remember one sentence: a class's identity is its name plus its loader, so the same name from different loaders means different classes, which is how app servers and plugins achieve isolation.
